steps.text: Vectors describe directions and displacements in space – and are the entry point to linear algebra. In many school types analytic geometry is neglected. This chapter builds it from the ground up.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. Calculating with vectors, length and distance
2. Dot product: angle, orthogonality, projection
3. Cross product: normal vector, area
4. Lines and planes in space, relative positions, distances
steps.insight: A vector is a tuple of numbers – and at the same time an arrow. Both views are equivalent and complement each other.

steps.text: Vectors are added component by component. Geometrically you attach the arrows end to end. Scalar multiplication stretches or compresses the arrow.
steps.explanation:
The animation shows \(v = (2, 1)\) and \(w = (1, 2)\): attach \(w\) to the tip of \(v\), and \(v + w = (3, 3)\) is the arrow from the origin to the new tip.

The connecting vector from \(A\) to \(B\) is "tip minus tail": \(\overrightarrow{AB} = B - A\). Example: \(A = (1, 2)\), \(B = (4, 6)\): \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (3, 4)\).

Rules as with numbers: \(a + b = b + a\), \(\lambda(a + b) = \lambda a + \lambda b\). The zero vector changes nothing, \(-a\) reverses the arrow.
steps.insight: Point and position vector are interchangeable: the point \(P(3, 4)\) has the position vector \(\overrightarrow{OP} = (3, 4)\).

steps.text: The length (magnitude) of a vector follows from the Pythagorean theorem. Dividing by the length gives a vector of length \(1\) – the unit vector.
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• \(|(3, 4)| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\), the unit vector is \(\left(\frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{5}\right)\).
• \(|(1, 2, 2)| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3\).
• Distance of \(A(1, 2, 3)\) and \(B(4, 6, 3)\): \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (3, 4, 0)\), so \(d = 5\).

We have \(|\lambda v| = |\lambda|\,|v|\) and the triangle inequality \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\).
steps.insight: The length of a vector in space is Pythagoras in two steps: first the diagonal of the base, then the space diagonal.

steps.text: The dot product of two vectors is a NUMBER. It has two equivalent descriptions – a computational and a geometric one:
steps.formula: a \cdot b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3 = |a|\,|b|\cos\varphi
steps.explanation:
Example \(a = (2, 1)\), \(b = (1, 2)\): \(a \cdot b = 2 + 2 = 4\). Both have length \(\sqrt{5}\). From \(4 = \sqrt{5} \cdot \sqrt{5}\cos\varphi\) we get \(\cos\varphi = \frac{4}{5}\), so \(\varphi \approx 36.9°\).

The dot product immediately reveals the relative position:
• \(a \cdot b = 0\) \(\iff\) \(a \perp b\) (orthogonal), e.g. \((2, -1) \cdot (1, 2) = 0\).
• \(a \cdot b > 0\): acute angle, \(a \cdot b < 0\): obtuse angle.

Angle formula: \(\cos\varphi = \frac{a \cdot b}{|a|\,|b|}\).
steps.insight: You check orthogonality with the dot product – not with the angle. \(a \cdot b = 0\) is a simple equation.

steps.text: The geometric meaning: the dot product measures how much of \(b\) points in the direction of \(a\). You project \(b\) perpendicularly onto the line through \(a\).
steps.explanation:
The animation shows \(a = (4, 0)\) and \(b = (3, 2)\): the perpendicular from the tip of \(b\) onto the line through \(a\) lands at \((3, 0)\). Calculation: \(a \cdot b = 12\), \(|a|^2 = 16\), so \(\text{proj}_a(b) = \frac{12}{16}(4, 0) = (3, 0)\) ✓.

The remainder \(b - \text{proj}_a(b) = (0, 2)\) is perpendicular to \(a\): \((0, 2) \cdot (4, 0) = 0\) ✓.

Applications: work \(W = F \cdot s\) (only the force component along the path does work), distance of a point from a line, decomposing a vector into parallel and perpendicular parts.
steps.insight: The dot product is symmetric (\(a \cdot b = b \cdot a\)) and linear. But careful: \(a \cdot b \cdot c\) is undefined – a scalar times a vector is not.

steps.text: In space there is additionally the cross product: it gives for two vectors a third one that is perpendicular to both.
steps.formula: a \times b = \begin{pmatrix} a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2 \\ a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3 \\ a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad |a \times b| = |a|\,|b|\sin\varphi
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• \((1, 0, 0) \times (0, 1, 0) = (0, 0, 1)\) – the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes span the \(z\)-direction.
• \((1, 2, 3) \times (4, 5, 6) = (12 - 15,\ 12 - 6,\ 5 - 8) = (-3, 6, -3)\).

Properties:
• \(a \times b\) is perpendicular to \(a\) and to \(b\) (check with the dot product: \((1, 2, 3) \cdot (-3, 6, -3) = -3 + 12 - 9 = 0\) ✓).
• Anticommutative: \(b \times a = -(a \times b)\). And \(a \times a = 0\).
• Length \(= \) area of the parallelogram spanned by \(a\) and \(b\). The triangle has half the area: \(\frac{1}{2}|a \times b|\).

For \((1, 2, 3)\) and \((4, 5, 6)\): \(|a \times b| = \sqrt{9 + 36 + 9} = \sqrt{54} \approx 7.35\).
steps.insight: The order in the cross product matters – swapping reverses the direction. The dot product, in contrast, is symmetric.

steps.text: A line in space is determined by a position vector \(p\) (anchor point) and a direction vector \(u\):
steps.explanation:
Line through \(A(1, 2, 3)\) and \(B(3, 2, 5)\): anchor \(A\), direction \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (2, 0, 2)\):
\(g: \ x = (1, 2, 3) + t\,(2, 0, 2)\).

Point check: does \(P(5, 2, 7)\) lie on \(g\)? From the first coordinate \(1 + 2t = 5\) we get \(t = 2\); then the second \(2\) ✓ and the third \(3 + 4 = 7\) ✓. Yes.
\(Q(2, 2, 3)\)? First coordinate: \(t = 0.5\); third: \(3 + 1 = 4 \neq 3\). No.

In the plane a single equation suffices: \(ax + by = c\) (coordinate form) or \(y = mx + n\).
steps.insight: Parametric form: determine \(t\) from ONE coordinate and then check all the others.

steps.text: Two lines in space have four possible positions: identical, parallel, intersecting or skew (neither parallel nor sharing a point).
steps.explanation:
Procedure:
1. Are the direction vectors multiples of each other? Then parallel or identical (point check!).
2. Otherwise equate: \(1 + t = 2\), \(2 + t = 3 + s\), \(t = 1 + 2s\) (three equations for \(t, s\)).
   From the first \(t = 1\); the second gives \(s = 0\); the third: \(1 = 1\) ✓. There is an intersection point \((2, 3, 1)\).
3. If the system is unsolvable and the directions are not parallel, the lines are skew.

Skew example: \(g: t(1, 0, 0)\) and \(h: (0, 1, 0) + s(0, 0, 1)\). The directions differ, and \(g\) has \(y = 0\), \(h\) has \(y = 1\) – never a common point.
steps.insight: Skew lines exist only in space. In the plane two non-parallel lines always intersect.

steps.text: A plane is determined by a point and two directions or by a point and a normal vector \(n\). The normal form leads directly to the coordinate equation:
steps.formula: n \cdot (x - p) = 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad n_1 x_1 + n_2 x_2 + n_3 x_3 = d
steps.explanation:
Plane through \(A(1, 0, 0)\), \(B(0, 1, 0)\), \(C(0, 0, 1)\):
• Directions: \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (-1, 1, 0)\), \(\overrightarrow{AC} = (-1, 0, 1)\).
• Normal vector: \(n = \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = (1, 1, 1)\).
• Equation: \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = d\). Substituting \(A\): \(d = 1\).

So \(E: \ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1\). Check: \(B\) and \(C\) satisfy the equation ✓.

Two planes are perpendicular when their normal vectors are orthogonal.
steps.insight: The cross product of two direction vectors gives the normal vector – the standard way from parametric to coordinate form.

steps.text: Distances with the normal form: the distance of a point \(P\) from the plane \(n_1 x_1 + n_2 x_2 + n_3 x_3 = d\) is
steps.formula: d(P, E) = \frac{|n \cdot P - d|}{|n|}, \qquad d(P, \text{line } ax + by = c) = \frac{|a x_0 + b y_0 - c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• Plane \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1\), point \(P(2, 2, 2)\): \(\frac{|6 - 1|}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 2.89\).
• Line \(3x + 4y = 12\), point \((0, 0)\): \(\frac{|0 - 12|}{5} = \frac{12}{5} = 2.4\).

Intersection of a line with a plane: substitute the parametric representation of the line into the coordinate equation. \(g: t\,(1, 1, 1)\) and \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 3\): \(3t = 3\), so \(t = 1\) and \(S = (1, 1, 1)\).
steps.insight: If substituting gives \(0 = 0\), the line lies in the plane; \(0 = c\) with \(c \neq 0\): line parallel to the plane, no intersection.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Add and scale vectors component by component. \(\overrightarrow{AB} = B - A\), \(|v| = \sqrt{\sum v_i^2}\), unit vector \(\frac{v}{|v|}\).

2. Dot product: \(a \cdot b = \sum a_i b_i = |a||b|\cos\varphi\). \(a \cdot b = 0 \iff a \perp b\). Projection \(\frac{a \cdot b}{|a|^2} a\).

3. Cross product: perpendicular to both, length = parallelogram area, anticommutative.

4. Line \(p + tu\), plane \(n \cdot (x - p) = 0\). Position of two lines: identical, parallel, intersecting, skew.

5. Distance point–plane \(\frac{|n \cdot P - d|}{|n|}\). Intersection line–plane by substitution.
steps.insight: Congratulations! In "Vector Spaces" the arrow becomes a general object, in "Matrices" and "Linear Mappings" systems of equations and rotations are described with vectors – all on this foundation.
